The problem with the question "How do you conquer depression?" is that it's like asking "How do you fix a broken down car?"

Well, it depends on what's wrong with the car. There are dozens of different things that might be the cause for your car breaking down, and there are probably 1000 different things that could be causing and/or contributing to your depression. The first step in conquering your depression as you put it, would be to spend some significant time and energy trying to identify what are the specific factors that have been leading to depression.

It could be one thing, or a dozen, but knowing what triggers your depression and what intensifies it is critical in making lasting improvement.

Similarly, identifying things that can help with improving your depression is important as well. Triggers and factors that can lift your mental state and mood. Sometimes these can be hard to find, and sometimes they are readily available. The more of them you know about and can make use of, the better position you will be in with regards to fighting depression.

Start small. Originally I started with 10 minutes daily when I first woke up (well, after turning on the lights and using the bathroom).

The key is accepting that you're going to think, the point of meditation isn't to stop thinking. If there was a way to stop thinking everyone would be doing it. Instead what you need to do is find an anchor, for a lot of people it's their breath, for others their heart beat, and others use a mantra (repeating a phrase or syllables over and over).

From there, you simply sit, eyes closed or partially closed, and observe. If you find yourself lost in a thought, without judgement just go back to your anchor. If all you do is think, go back to your anchor, think again, go back to your anchor for the entire 10 minutes then cogradualtions you're meditating.

Once you can sit for 10 minutes there's a whole world of possibilities and techniques to explore. From labeling techniques, visualizations, breathing techniques, mantras, etc.

I personally use the app Headspace, but there's a lot of free apps, plus YouTube has plenty of free guided meditations that can teach you new techniques. Most yoga classes end with meditation as well, and the teachers teach different techniques. When I first started I would go to a meditation group once a week as well.

Eventually you can bump up how long you meditate. Took me a few months to work up to 20 minutes.

Most important thing is to practice daily. Make a routine or habit. Studies have shown that daily meditation literally changes how the brain functions. Essentially you're creating a resting state of plasticity in the brain that helps regulate how the brain works.
